newsitem.title: UK: Differences between British parties hard to find.
newsitem.headline: Differences between British parties hard to find.

text.p: As Britain's election campaign begins, the two main parties are highlighting for voters the policy differences that separate them.

But in a number of key areas these differences have narrowed dramatically as a result of Labour Party leader Tony Blair's determined drive to reposition his once left-wing party, in opposition since 1979, in the political mainstream.
Following is a summary of the positions staked out by Labour and by Prime Minister John Major's Conservative party in five areas polls say could be crucial in swaying undecided voters.
EDUCATION -- The two parties have been leapfrogging each other with broadly similar initiatives to raise school standards and improve classroom discipline.

Labour fell into line with the government in December 1995 by dropping its opposition to the publication of performance tables for secondary schools. It then stole a march by proposing national reading targets and the dismissal of substandard teachers -- measures subsequently matched by the government.
Crucial differences on whether schools should be allowed to select pupils have also become blurred.

Labour still opposes any extension of selection by academic ability, but has backed off plans to close down existing selective schools (grammar schools) and will not shut schools that have opted for funding by central government rather than local authorities.

TAX AND SPENDING -- Labour's economics spokesman, Gordon Brown, threw the Conservatives into disarray in January not only by promising to freeze income tax rates but also by adopting their public spending plans for the next two years.

The bold stroke was intended to bury Labour's reputation as a party of high taxes and high spending and has forced the Conservatives to focus their attacks on Labour's plan to levy a one-off tax on the excess profits of privatised utilities.
Labour says it would use the levy to fund a three billion pound ($4.8 billion) programme aimed at getting 250,000 young unemployed people off welfare and into work.
Another clear difference on economic policy is Labour's pledge to introduce a national minimum wage.
EUROPE - Both major parties are committed to holding a referendum to endorse any future cabinet decision to join the European Union's planned single currency.
Both have also virtually ruled out joining the currency when it is launched in 1999 but Labour is more open to the possibility of joining later if the project succeeds.
Both parties oppose the emergence of a European superstate or the surrender of the British veto.
One key policy difference is the EU social chapter on workplace standards, which Labour says it would sign. The Conservatives say that to do so would cost half a million British jobs.
CONSTITUTIONAL REFORM - This is the area where the two main parties most clearly disagree.

The Conservatives say Labour plans for a Scottish parliament with the right to levy taxes (alongside a Welsh assembly) not only would impose a "tartan tax" north of the border, but also could lead to the break-up of the United Kingdom.
The ruling party is also scathing about Labour proposals to strip hereditary peers of the right to vote in the House of Lords, arguing that the upper chamber of parliament works well.
HEALTH -- Major made a splash at last October's Conservative conference by promising to increase spending on the National Health Service in real terms in each year of the next five-year parliament.
Labour has not matched that pledge but it has endorsed the government's spending plans for the next two years.
It also plans to reduce NHS administrative costs by 100 million pounds, which it says will pay for the treatment of an extra 100,000 patients.
It believes it can cut red tape by replacing the competitive 'internal market' set up by the Conservatives with a more integrated, cooperative system for commissioning healthcare.

But analysts doubt the changes would make much of an impact unless Labour is prepared to spend more, especially as the government's budget envisages only a 0.2 percent real increase in NHS spending in 1998-99, well below the historical trend of three percent a year. ($ = 0.624 British Pounds)
